analysis.one_liner: Creates a universal government health plan covering all U.S. residents, replacing Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, and most private insurance.
analysis.headline: Referred to five House committees on March 2, 2015 and given only subcommittee referrals; it never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a state-run American Health Security Program guaranteeing comprehensive health coverage — hospital care, doctor visits, prescription drugs, dental, vision, mental health, and long-term care — to every U.S. citizen and lawful resident, with no premiums, deductibles, or balance billing. It would end Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, federal employee coverage, and TRICARE as of the end of 2016, and bar the sale of private insurance that duplicates the public plan. It would be financed by an employer payroll tax, a new individual health care income tax, a surcharge on income above $1 million, and a tax on securities transactions.
analysis.who_benefits: Every U.S. citizen and lawful resident would receive comprehensive health coverage with no premiums, deductibles, or surprise charges, including services many current plans exclude: dental care, eyeglasses and hearing aids, long-term and home-based care, and prescription drugs. People with employer plans, Medicare, Medicaid, or no coverage at all would all be enrolled automatically.
analysis.who_benefits_short: All U.S. residents with any immigration status

how_it_helps.text: Entitles every U.S. citizen, national, and lawful resident alien to comprehensive covered services including hospital care, professional services, prescription drugs, dental, preventive care, mental health and substance abuse treatment, and long-term care.

Prohibits any charge for covered services beyond what the program pays — no balance billing — and limits new-resident waiting periods to no more than three months, with benefits portable across states.

Finances the program through an American Health Security Trust Fund supplied by an employer payroll tax, a health care income tax, a surcharge on income above $1 million, a securities transaction tax, and redirected existing Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, and Affordable Care Act spending.

analysis.who_pays: Employers pay a new payroll tax; individuals pay a health care income tax; households earning over $1 million pay a surcharge; financial firms pay a tax on securities trades. The health insurance industry loses most of its market, since private coverage duplicating the public plan is banned.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers, high earners, financial firms, insurers

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes substantial new taxes — an employer payroll tax, a health care income tax on individuals, a surcharge on income above $1 million, and an excise tax on securities transactions — shifting most health financing onto taxpayers.

The transition eliminates Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, Federal Employees Health Benefits, and TRICARE coverage for services after December 31, 2016, moving tens of millions of people with existing coverage into a new, untested program.

The new program has its own limits: long-term home and community-based care spending is capped relative to nursing facility costs, mental health inpatient and residential days are capped, and adult dental treatment is phased in over years.
States must prohibit the sale of private health insurance that duplicates program benefits, ending the option of buying comprehensive private coverage alongside the public plan.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is large and direct: universal, comprehensive coverage with no premiums or point-of-care charges, including services like dental and long-term care that most current plans skimp on. The costs are equally large and real: major new taxes across employers, individuals, high earners, and financial transactions, plus a one-time disruption that eliminates five existing health programs and most private insurance at once. Whether the trade pays off depends heavily on details the bill leaves to a new federal board, such as payment rates and global hospital budgets that would cut hospital revenues from current levels.

outcome.mechanism: Sitting on the shelf: the bill was referred to five House committees, sent to subcommittees, and was never given a hearing, markup, or vote for the rest of the Congress.

narrative.text: Representative Jim McDermott introduced the American Health Security Act of 2015 on March 2, 2015.
It was referred the same day to five House committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Oversight and Government Reform, Armed Services, and Education and the Workforce.

Between March and August 2015 it was referred to subcommittees on Health, Health Employment Labor and Pensions, Early Childhood Education, and Military Personnel; no further action of any kind appears in the record through the end of the 114th Congress.
The bill attracted exactly one cosponsor, a Democrat, in two years.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo and the industries that depend on it: private insurers kept their market, employers kept their current coverage arrangements, and no new health taxes were enacted. Nobody who lacked coverage gained anything.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private insurers and the health-care status quo

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a floor vote, so party splits were never measured; its sponsor and lone cosponsor were both Democrats, and no Republican support appears anywhere in the record.

industries.note: Each state must ban the sale of private insurance that duplicates the public plan's benefits, which would eliminate most of the private health insurance market. Insurers sit between patients and care and profit from that role; the bill would remove them from it.

Prescription drugs would be paid under program-set payment rules (Sec. 615) rather than negotiated against private insurers, ending the pricing power drug companies hold over Medicare Part D and private plans.

Hospitals would be paid through approved global budgets instead of per-service billing: less revenue than current billed charges, but no uncompensated care, no bad debt, and no balance billing against patients. Whether hospitals come out ahead depends entirely on the budgets set.

A new excise tax on securities transactions helps fund the program and adds a cost to every trade; the industry's interest in avoiding the tax runs against the public's interest in the funding it provides.
Employers would pay a new payroll tax but would be relieved of funding most employee health coverage, a benefit they currently finance; the two effects work in opposite directions.
An income tax surcharge on modified adjusted gross income above $1 million is a dedicated funding source for the program.
